title: Retail stocks: how to analyze retail companies
description: Retail stocks: thin margin, huge volume. How to compute capital turnover, like-for-like and the inventory clock — H&M, Inditex and Axfood in numbers.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Retail stocks are shares in companies that sell goods directly to consumers — in stores, online, or both. The sector runs from global fashion to Swedish groceries, and one property sets it apart: the margin is thin, the volume enormous, and profit is built where they intersect. A grocer keeping 2.7 kronor of every hundred-krona note in sales can still deliver over 30 percent return on equity — the capital in stores turns over many times a year. This guide covers the mechanics: three business models, the math of capital turnover, like-for-like growth, the inventory clock, the store estate as debt.

## Retail stocks — three business models, three margin worlds

The universe's three pure retailers show the range. H&M, the global fashion chain, reports a gross margin of 54.1 percent — of every hundred kronor sold, just over 54 is kept after the cost of goods. Inditex, Zara's Spanish parent, sits at 56.5 percent. Axfood, Swedish groceries, at 14.8. The difference reflects what sits on the shelf, not operational quality: fashion carries a high markup over purchase price; food is a volume commodity where price is compared every day.

Yet all three land at nearly the same return on equity: H&M 34.7, Inditex 34.0, Axfood 36.3 percent. Retail's key lesson in one row: there is more than one road to profitability, and the margin by itself decides nothing. The fashion company earns a lot per kronor sold; the grocer earns little but makes each kronor work far more turns a year — which mechanism carries a company shows when you decompose the return.

## Margin and volume — the two wheels of returns

ROE decomposes into two wheels: net profit per kronor of sales, and how many times equity turns over. The second wheel: market cap divided by the P/B ratio gives equity; sales divided by equity gives capital turnover.

Axfood: market cap SEK 53.1 billion, P/B 7.5 — equity 53.1 ÷ 7.5 ≈ 7.1 billion. Sales of 89.2 billion give capital turnover 89.2 ÷ 7.1 ≈ 12.6 times a year. With the 2.7 percent net margin: 2.7 % × 12.6 ≈ 34 percent — the bulk of the 36.3 ROE. H&M the same way: market cap 275.5 ÷ 8.1 ≈ 34 billion, sales 228.3 billion, capital turnover 6.7; 5.6 % × 6.7 ≈ 37. Two working businesses with almost mirror-image mechanics. The deep dive: [how to calculate ROE](/blogg/hur-raknar-man-roe) and the course [ROE — return on equity](/kurser/v09-roe).

The margin's fragility shows in a markdown example. A fashion company with gross profit of 54 per 100 kronor of sales and operating profit of 11 marks down a tenth of the goods 30 percent: gross profit falls to 51 and operating profit to 8 — a price change on a small part of the range wipes out more than a quarter of the profit. That is retail's operating leverage — why the gross margin's quarterly movement is the sector's most important line. The whole chain from purchasing to markdown: [the gross margin methodology](/kurser/v07-bruttomarginal) and [gross margin analysis](/blogg/v07-bruttomarginal-analys).

## Like-for-like — the two sources of growth

Retailers can grow two ways: open more stores, or sell more in existing ones. The measure of the latter is like-for-like — sales development in comparable units — and the difference between them determines whether growth is organic or bought with the capital cost of expansion.

H&M's 2022–2025 series shows the reverse journey: sales fell from 236.0 to 228.3 billion, but profit rose from 3.6 to 12.2 billion — more than a tripling on falling revenue. The profit was created in the margin — cost control, assortment reshaping, fewer markdowns — not in volume. A classic sector observation: the income statement can turn before revenue does. The full walkthrough: [the analysis of H&M](/blogg/analys-h-och-m-hennes-och-mauritz-2026). Axfood shows the opposite profile: sales grew from 73.5 to 89.2 billion 2022–2025 (+6.7 percent per year) while profit stayed essentially flat around 2.3 billion — volume rose, but price competition in Swedish food retail took the growth out of the margin. Inditex grew in both sales (+5.8 percent, latest twelve months) and profitability. Three companies, three combinations of the same two variables.

## Inventory — the clock of fashion retail

In fashion, much of the risk lives in the inventory: clothes not sold at full price must be marked down, and each markdown eats the gross margin. The measure is inventory turnover — cost of goods sold divided by average inventory — how many times the stock is replaced per year. Faster turnover: fewer markdowns and write-downs, less capital tied up in goods. Rising inventory days on weak sales is retail's earliest warning: the problem shows up in the balance sheet before the income statement.

The Inditex–H&M contrast explains what actually separates them. Gross margins sit close — 56.5 versus 54.1 percent — but operating margins differ by more than nine percentage points: 20.1 versus 11.0. The difference lives on the cost side, not the price tag: Inditex's vertically integrated model with short lead times from design to store hits demand better, giving fewer markdowns and more full-price sales. Same gross margin, double operating margin — the difference between selling the right item and selling the item right.

## The balance sheet — the store estate as debt

Since IFRS 16 leases are capitalized, changing the picture of retail: the store estate appears as debt. H&M reports debt to equity of 2.26 and Axfood 2.24, while Inditex sits at 0.32 — partly because the Spanish group owns many flagship stores instead of leasing them. Read it as structure rather than pure risk, but the content is real: leases are fixed obligations paid regardless of sales — the same mechanics as interest cost. A heavy rent burden adds another layer of operating leverage on top of the markdown mechanism. The foundations: [the balance sheet in 15 minutes](/blogg/sa-laser-du-en-balansrakning-pa-15-minuter), [the debt-to-equity methodology](/kurser/v10-skuldsattningsgrad) and [which debt level is dangerous](/blogg/skuldsattningsgrad-vilken-niva-ar-farlig).

The thin capital base has a valuation consequence: P/B ratios of 7.5–9.3 among the three are not in themselves overvaluation — they follow directly from equity being small relative to sales. The multiple reflects the business model's capital turnover — comparing book values correctly is covered in [interpreting the P/B ratio](/blogg/pb-tal-nar-jamfor-man-bokvarde-ratt).

## How to structure your reading of the report

- **Like-for-like against total growth.** Expansion can conceal weak organic development; the two numbers show which growth costs capex.
- **The gross margin's movement.** Quarter on quarter, against the same quarter last year — markdown alarm and pricing-power thermometer in one.
- **Inventory turnover.** Rising inventory on flat sales is the sector's earliest warning.
- **Store openings and capex.** Expansion is paid in cash in the investing cash flow; note also closures and renegotiated leases.
- **Channel and currency mix.** E-commerce margin against the store's, and the currencies in a global fashion company's sales.

A valuation note: the PEG ratio — P/E divided by forecast growth — carries a built-in distortion in low-growth retail. Axfood's P/E of 21.9 against forecast earnings growth of 8.4 percent gives a PEG of 2.6 — formally expensive-looking, but reflecting a defensive, dividend-bearing business rather than a rich valuation; the pitfalls are walked through in [the weaknesses of the PEG multiple](/blogg/peg-multipeln-svagheter-2026). Rather compare multiples against the company's own history and sector peers, as in [relative valuation](/kurser/km-011-relativ-vardering), and read reports with [the quarterly reading order](/kurser/km-006-kvartalsrapporten) as backbone. The sector's own walkthrough: the course [the retail sector](/kurser/se-07-detailhandel).

## Summary

- Three margin worlds: fashion 54–56 percent gross against groceries 14.8 — the difference is business model, not quality.
- Return = margin × capital turnover: Axfood turns capital 12.6 times a year, H&M 6.7.
- Like-for-like separates organic growth from store expansion; H&M more than tripled profit on falling sales.
- Inventory is the clock: Inditex earns double H&M's operating margin on nearly the same gross margin.
- IFRS 16 makes the store estate debt — read debt/equity as structure, and P/B against capital turnover.
